title: Death doesn't wait its turn
translation: If you want to get on in the world, the first thing to learn is timing. Bring something up at the wrong moment and people won't want to hear it. It rubs them the wrong way, and it gets nowhere. You need a feel for when.

Only three things don't care about timing: falling ill, having a baby, and dying. They don't hold off because the moment is wrong. Everything is born, stays a while, changes and ends, and that change is the one thing that really matters. It's like a river in flood. It never stops, not even for a moment. It just keeps going. So whether it's about the Buddha's path or your everyday life, if there's something you really mean to get done, don't talk about timing. Don't wait until you're ready. Don't stand still.

Spring doesn't end and then turn into summer, and autumn doesn't wait for summer to finish. Spring is already bringing on the summer air. Autumn is already there inside summer. Autumn gets cold right away, and then in early winter there are mild, sunny days, the grass turns green again and the plum trees bud. Leaves don't fall first and then the new buds come. The buds are already swelling underneath, the old leaves can't hold on any longer, and they fall. The new thing is ready and waiting below, so the change comes very fast.

Birth, old age, sickness and death come even faster than that. The seasons at least keep to an order. Death doesn't wait its turn. It doesn't come at you from the front. It's been right behind you all along. Everyone knows they're going to die, but they don't feel it's urgent, and then it comes before they notice. Out on the mud flats, the sea looks far away. Meanwhile, the tide is coming in at the shore.

literal: A person who would go along with the world should first know the right moment.
Things out of order go against people's ears and against their hearts, and the thing does not succeed; one should understand such occasions.
However, only falling ill, giving birth and dying do not consider the right moment, and do not stop because the order is bad.
The truly great matter, the shifting and changing of arising, abiding, changing and perishing, is like a fierce river swelling and flowing.
It does not stop even for a moment, but goes straight on.
So, in the sacred and the secular alike, of a thing that one means to accomplish without fail, one should not speak of the right moment.
With no preparations of this or that, one should not stop one's feet.
It is not that summer comes after spring has ended, and autumn comes when summer is over.

Spring soon brings on the air of summer, from summer autumn already passes in, autumn at once turns cold, the tenth month has the weather of little spring, the grass too turns green, and the plum too has buds.
The falling of tree leaves, too, is not that they first fall and then sprout; they fall because they cannot withstand the budding and swelling from below.
Because the energy that will receive it is prepared below, the order of waiting and taking over is very quick.
The coming on of birth, old age, sickness and death goes beyond even this.
The four seasons still have a fixed order.
The time of death does not wait for the order.
Death does not come from in front; it is already pressing from behind.
Everyone knows that there is death, and while their waiting for it is not urgent, it comes without their noticing.
It is like the tide filling in from the shore, though the tidal flats offshore are far.

notes.text: A false friend: {機嫌|きげん} here is 'the right moment, the circumstances', not modern 'mood'. It was a Buddhist word first. {序|ついで} in the next sentence means 'order, turn': the right point in a sequence.
{逆|さか}ふ: 'to go against'. Things said at the wrong time go against people's ears.

{生住|しやうぢう}{異滅|いめつ}: a Buddhist term for the four phases of everything that exists: it arises, abides, changes and perishes. The 1925 edition reads it about human life instead: birth, living in a place, falling ill and changing shape, and death. The reading しやうぢう is printed as in the edition; the usual spelling is しやうぢゆう. {大事|だいじ}: 'the great matter', in Buddhist use the matter of life and death.
{真俗|しんぞく}: the sacred and the secular, Buddhist practice and ordinary life. The advice is for both.

{十月|かんなづき}: the tenth month of the old calendar, the first month of winter, about November today. {小春|こはる}: 'little spring', a run of mild days in early winter. Modern Japanese still says {小春日和|こはるびより}, much like 'Indian summer'.

notes.quote: 下より萌しつはるに堪へずして落つるなり
notes.text: {萌|きざ}す: 'to show the first signs'. つはる: 'to swell, to bud'; modern つわり, 'morning sickness', is usually derived from it. The old leaf does not fall to make room: it is pushed off by the new bud.
{生老|しやうらう}{病死|びやうし}: birth, old age, sickness and death, the four sufferings of Buddhism. The next lines contrast them with the seasons: the seasons keep their order, death does not.

notes.quote: 死は前よりしも来らず、かねて後に迫れり
notes.text: しも stresses the word before it: not from the front. かねて: 'already, beforehand'. {迫|せま}れり: {迫|せま}る + り, 'has been pressing'. Compare the end of section 137, where death is an army charging into the quiet mountains.

notes.quote: 沖の干潟遥かなれども、磯より潮の満つるが如し
notes.text: On a wide tidal flat, you look out and the sea is far away, while the water comes in at the shore. The section ends on this image, with no comment.
